stories.title: Irish 15-year-olds rank first for reading in EU - study
stories.summary: Ireland's 15-year-olds have ranked first for reading, third for science and fourth for mathematics out of the 27 EU countries, in a major international educational study. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) measures how well a cohort of 15-year-old students are doing in the three core domains of reading, mathematics and science. The study is conducted every four years, with the next cycle due in 2029. Students in Ireland also rated above the EU and OECD averages in computational problem solving. However, overall the report revealed that Irish students' performance in reading and mathematics is lower than in previous cycles of the study. In terms of PISA scores, declines were observed across all three core domains in the OECD and EU. Ireland also experienced such declines but to a lesser extent than the OECD or EU. While Ireland's performance was above the OECD and EU averages in all domains, the study revealed that there were considerably lower proportions of low performers, defined as students lacking key skills and competences in Ireland across all domains compared to the average across OECD and EU countries.

stories.title: Co Down victim conned out of £250k in AI investment scam
stories.summary: A person in Northern Ireland was scammed out of £250,000 (approximately €291,000) by what police have described as a "sophisticated" AI-generated investment fraud. It began after the Co Down-based victim responded to an online video featuring a well-known personality from the financial sector. It offered an investment opportunity with "significant" returns. After the victim had invested a relatively modest amount, they were contacted via Whatsapp and encouraged to put in more. The fraudsters then persuaded the person to create multiple online accounts and got remote access to their computer by pretending to help them with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow additional money to pour into the scheme.

stories.title: Fuel excise cuts should remain permanently, Tóibín says
stories.summary: Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín has said the Government needs to stop wasting taxpayers money and called for temporary cuts to fuel prices to be made permanent. Aontú is preparing for its annual think-in in Co Derry on Saturday. Mr Tóibín said fuel is a stable, and not a luxury, good and that it was astounding that there are half a million people in energy arrears in the country. He said: "In terms of capital infrastructure spends last year there was about €1.6bn of overspend. "There's a complete lack of accountability in that sector. There's an enormous amount of waste. "Indeed, I would say the Government is incinerating taxpayers' money at a rate in those terms.

stories.title: Are you a drunk online shopper?
stories.summary: Analysis: Drunk shopping is a rapidly growing consumption phenomenon where tipsy consumers are responsible for billions of euros in annual revenue One Sunday morning, Juliet* woke up to an eager delivery driver with a large package she had no recollection of ordering. She was quick to dismiss it as an e-commerce mistake before the card inside helped solve the mystery: "To Sober Juliet, from your friend, Drunk Juliet." The fact this story was recounted to us while researching this topic illustrates the rise of a cultural trend that surprisingly few academics have explored. But drunk shopping is a rapidly growing consumption phenomenon. Intoxicated consumers generate billions of dollars in annual revenue, which one US survey estimated to be around €38.7 billion a year. In research carried out with colleagues, we attempted to explore this phenomenon and its ethical implications further. When alcohol enters the human body, it acts as a general disinhibitor, causing people to "let go" of the inhibitions that would normally constrain their actions and increasing the likelihood of engaging in foolish and risky behaviour. Psychologists call the underlying mechanism alcohol myopia: short-sighted information processing that is part of alcohol intoxication. Alcohol reduces the scope and focus of attention, limiting both the range of cues that can be perceived and the ability to process them. Behaviour is based only on the most salient and impelling "go" cues in the environment, not the less salient and inhibiting "no go" ones. While driving, this might mean missing the dog running into the road; behind an electronic platform, it can mean that the inviting "buy now" button crowds out anything else on the screen. People shopping while drunk may pay a great deal of attention to the payment process at the expense of other significant details, such as the amount of money they will spend or the selection of a preferred item. And this is not ordinary impulse buying. We define drunk shopping as a context-specific form of impulse purchasing, distinct from consumption when tired or stressed. It reflects a situational, temporary impairment, not a chronic, trait-based vulnerability, such as being materialistic.

stories.title: Eiffel Tower to reopen after row on removing women staff
stories.summary: The Eiffel Tower is set to reopen today after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologised. The operating company that runs the Paris landmark, SETE, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted". It said the landmark is due to reopen on today following a meeting the previous day between staff and management. The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologised for "any pain or inconvenience caused" by the incident. "To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower," the organisation wrote on X. "Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others."

stories.title: Preston a 'brilliant fit' for Kenny but what of Moran?
stories.summary: Last week, a number of Republic of Ireland internationals were on the move before the summer transfer window slammed shut. Former Sligo Rovers and Shamrock Rovers striker Johnny Kenny was among that cohort, with the 23-year-old making a permanent move from Celtic to sign for Preston North End and making his debut as a substitute on Saturday. The English Championship outfit is one of Keith Treacy's former clubs and the ex-Republic of Ireland winger is hopeful that Kenny will be able to find stability in Lancashire. "So Johnny going there, if he misses one or two chances, (the fans) are quite forgiving. "But it's a brilliant, brilliant place Preston. I really liked it. "He'll enjoy it, it's a brilliant club, well run, the training ground has been upgraded, so good luck and I hope he does really well."

stories.title: Club round-up: Kobe returns to help Crossmolina advance
stories.summary: Kobe McDonald returned to the Mayo senior football championship as Crossmolina Deel Rovers just did enough to qualify for the quarter-finals. McDonald, who departed for St Kilda in the AFL in the wake of Mayo's seismic All-Ireland victory, has been granted permission to feature in the club championship back home and he kicked 0-03 as his Crossmolina side held on for a draw against Mayo Gaels and advanced to the last-eight at Ballintubber's expense. It was a nervier affair than expected for the 2001 All-Ireland champions against the group's bottom-placed team. McDonald scored the first point of the game, adding two from placed balls after half-time. But they needed a late equaliser for Jordan Flynn to snatch a 0-16 to 2-10 draw and progress in second place. Ryan O'Donoghue's Beal an Mhuirthead dispatched Ballaghaderreen 4-17 to 2-13 to advance to an away quarter-final in second place, with Breaffy's comfortable victory over Knockmore condemning the latter to a group stage exit. There will be new champions in Mayo as four-in-a-row chasing Ballina Stephenites had already been eliminated with a round to spare, with Garrymore and Castlebar Mitchels progressing from a fraught Group 2. In the Dublin SFC, Kilmacud Crokes narrowly survived the group stage after their five-point win over Ballinteer St John's was just about sufficient to book their spot in the quarters.

stories.title: Round up: Ulster and Connacht bag first pre-season wins
stories.summary: Ulster and Connacht recorded their first pre-season victories in two tense tussles over the weekend. On Friday night, Richie Murphy's Ulster scraped past fellow URC challengers Edinburgh in Scotland, three weeks prior to their opening league clash on 25 September. As for Connacht, they were big winners over English CHAMP side Ealing Trailfinders, whose squad featured four Irish players. Ulster got their pre-season campaign off to an ideal start with a narrow two-point victory over Edinburgh in the Hive Stadium on Friday night. Debutant half-backs Jamie Benson and Matthew Devine combined for 11 points, with the former Connacht man scoring a first-half try, as Ulster raced into a 14 point lead after just 25 minutes. With a 27-man travelling squad named by Richie Murphy, all eyes were on the plentiful supply of new faces. Benson and Devine combined at half-back, Daniel Hawkshaw and Chay Mullins also started in the backline with Eduardo Bello, Ben Donnell, Eli Snyman and Martin Moloney all among the replacements. Academy prospects Flynn Longstaff and Jed Findlay rounded off the debutants from the bench also. The visitors raced into an early lead helped by set-piece dominance. A scrum penalty win led to the first try, with hooker James McCormick dotting down from the back of a powerful rolling maul. Edinburgh responded with a try of their own courtesy of centre Geordie Gwynn, but then came Ulster's gear change.

stories.title: Inside George Lucas's spectacular new Museum of Narrative Arts
stories.summary: As I sit in the Metro train heading towards South Los Angeles on the morning of September 2nd, I find my destination is evoking all kinds of childhood memories, writes Brian Lally. I have been invited to a media preview of the new Lucas Museum, a sprawling, futuristic building dedicated to narrative art. But what exactly do we mean by the term narrative art? It is art whose main purpose is to support a story, whether that takes the form of designs for spaceships for Star Wars films, or magazine and comic book illustrations from throughout the twentieth century, or even prehistoric cave art, and just about everything in between. Many of these exhibits in the museum are drawn from the massive personal collection of George Lucas himself. Despite the breadth of this collection, the Star Wars section dominates my anticipation; I find myself thinking back to all the films I have seen. Which is my favourite? Is it the first one from 1977, A New Hope, or the bleak 1980 sequel, The Empire Strikes Back? It's certainly not the one with the Ewoks, nor that second wave of films from the late 90s, though they did have their moments. Some of the more recent ones are good, but I saw them as an adult, not as a wide-eyed child, so the experience was never going to be magical, no matter how well made they were. Then a chill ran down my spine. Oh, no, what about Jar Jar Binks from The Phantom Menace? — The most irritating character in the Star Wars universe. He might be there somewhere. It's like you are going to a party and you start to realise that someone you despise might be there and can’t be avoided. Please George, no Jar Jar today. The E line Metro takes me to Exposition Park, an area of LA which contains several museums and a football stadium. As I crossed the road towards the Lucas Centre, above the trees, I get a glimpse of its distinctive curved roof and then it starts — a feeling of schoolboy-like excitement. As a world-weary, middle-aged man, this sensation was both nostalgic and pleasant. Having attended primary school way back in the 1970s, I remember the various waves of near hysteria that used to grip our classroom in relation to the Star Wars films. I remember one boy was accused of shouting "Star Wars, here I come!" as his parents took him to the Savoy cinema in Dublin. Even amongst excitable schoolboys, over-excitement of that calibre was considered naff, and he spent the rest of the term denying he ever said that. As for me, as I was ushered past security, I did find myself privately thinking "Lucas Centre, here I come", and my general state could be described as - if you'll pardon the language - giddy as f**k. The first thing that impresses is the Lucas Centre building itself. It looks like a spacecraft has just hovered over LA and softly landed in Exposition Park. The flowing, streamlined form reminds me of the sleek, aerodynamic spacecraft of the Planet Naboo from The Phantom Menace, which look like they had been somehow designed in the 1940s. As the place is full of media people, television reporters and podcasters, I hear certain phrases being eagerly shouted into cameras and microphones. One sentiment is clearly being repeated — the building itself is a work of art. I would agree with that. The building is a pleasing organic spectacle of flowing curves, totally devoid of right angles, straight lines, or hard edges, and set in green parkland — an antidote to LA’s many forgettable LEGO office blocks, soulless strip malls, and the asphalt parking lots which this site once was. The architect would later speak at the event and said the building was inspired by a cloud.

stories.title: Why breaking up was the best thing Oasis ever did
stories.summary: Don't Look Back in Anger, the new film about the Oasis reunion, hits real emotional high notes as it tells the story of their miraculous comeback tour. As Noel says, "It turns out that the Oasis thing never went away . . . " Ten years ago, director Mat Whitecross gave us Supersonic, a terrific rock doc about the rise of Oasis from Burnage dreamers to Britrock royalty in the space of just three meteoric years. Tinged with regret, sadness and not a little anger from then-estranged brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, it was a great film about ambition and rock 'n' roll excess and success that really got into the pain and glory of being in a massive band. Supersonic ended in 1996 on a considerable high with two headline gigs at Knebworth, but there was still a lot of the Oasis story to be told, not least their ignoble split backstage in Paris in 2009 in a final sibling meltdown involving a plum thrown in anger and Liam wielding one of Noel's favourite guitars like Excalibur. By 2016, both brothers had moved on to successful solo careers and the chances of a reunion looked very remote indeed, but here we are a decade later with a new Oasis film that chronicles what happened next and their miraculous comeback tour. To tell the biggest music story of the past five years, writer Steven Knight and co-directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace's (Shut Up and Play the Hits, Meet Me in the Bathroom) go all out with an epic rock 'n' roll road movie that spans 12 concerts over three continents. Given that this is Oasis, everything is on a huge scale, but at its heart, Don't Look Back in Anger is a very human story about forgiveness and redemption. As much as anything else, it is a life-affirming paean to the power of music itself and its mysterious ability to bring people together and heal, for both creators and fans alike. But there is a lot missing here. Shot in IMAX, it looks fantastic and is technically superb, but the whole film is so orchestrated and slick that it has the over-polished sheen of corporate spin. It has none of the punky raggedness of Whitecross's film, but that is to be expected. Anyone who witnessed this once most volatile of bands in action over two nights in Croke Park last year will know that we are now looking at the New Oasis; a tightly-drilled unit with dollar signs in their eyes. Anyone expecting bust-ups, tantrums and fisticuffs from this film will come away disappointed.

stories.title: Review: MG's S6 spacious family SUV
stories.summary: Irish car buyers have certainly embraced the crossover concept that makes many cars look like SUV's, even when they are only vaguely related, and manufacturers continue to meet the demand with more and more of them. The latest to come our way is the Chinese MG S6, which may lack the presence of a VW ID4, the sharp looks of a Skoda Enyaq or the bold design of a Kia EV 6, but it does have a shape that more than meets most peoples’ expectations and there’s nothing to dislike. Like other Chinese cars, it offers a very attractive package in terms of - you’ve guessed it - price and standard equipment. However, the MG offers one more advantage - space and lots of it. The front and back offer seriously good head and legroom and the cabin has a spacious and bright aspect. But for the rather large centre console (it houses the gearshift dial and phone charger) between the driver and passenger seat, the S6 offers excellent levels of comfort and the car has benefited from the use of premium-looking materials in the main. The entry-level version comes in at just under €40,000, which presents a challenge for its big name competitors. The MGS6 EV Exclusive Long Range version has more standard equipment and advanced features, such as the panoramic sunroof.

stories.title: Iran says it fired advanced missile at US warships
stories.summary: Iran has threatened the United States with "economic warfare" and said it had fired an advanced missile at US warships, underscoring the risks of further escalation in the war only days after both sides traded blows again. The ⁠six-month-old war has been marked by a cycle of pauses followed by periodic flare-ups, with the US last reporting attacks on Iranian targets on Saturday, when US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers. Iranian state media reported that Iran fired the Qassem Basir missile yesterday. Despite US attempts to open up the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has continued to disrupt shipping through the critical artery for global oil and gas supplies, and there is no sign of progress towards a diplomatic breakthrough that could end the war which began with US and Israeli strikes on 28 February. The Islamic Republic has vowed to announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, but it is unclear when details will emerge. The new restricted zone would begin from where the US blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television yesterday.

stories.title: AGSI rejects new Garda travel and subsistence scheme
stories.summary: Members of the Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors (AGSI) have voted overwhelmingly to reject a new Garda travel and subsistence scheme. Of the valid votes cast, 88.7% were against the proposed system. It followed more than six years of negotiations and engagement between AGSI and Garda management, including discussions at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). The AGSI said it accepted the scheme when it was published, on the understanding that it reflected the agreements reached during the WRC process. "However, serious concerns subsequently arose regarding management's interpretation and proposed implementation of the scheme," the association said. The AGSI added that, in its view, aspects of the approach moved away from what had been agreed during the WRC process.

stories.title: Border poll conditions 'have to be discussed' - Taoiseach
stories.summary: The conditions for calling a border poll is "an issue that has to be discussed", the Taoiseach has said. Issues relating to Northern Ireland are on the agenda for a meeting between Micheál Martin and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham later this month. Mr Burnham drew criticism when he said discussions on a border poll would be "off the table" as he visited Belfast at the end of August, later clarifying his remarks were about the day's engagements as he said he was committed to the Good Friday Agreement. Speaking at his party's think-in in Co Offaly, Mr Martin said: "He hasn’t said anything different to previous British prime ministers, and in our view, you know, we’ve got to continue to build on reconciliation, continue to build on increasing that connectivity, practical connectivity, north and south. "What’s important is that the Good Friday Agreement came about because of the British and Irish governments being anchors to that initiative, working with all the political parties, political traditions in the North and in the Republic, and so, in our view, the future has to be determined in that spirit and in that approach." Under the terms of the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement, the Secretary of State can decide to hold a border poll, and it also places a duty on the office holder to call one if it appears likely a majority would vote for Irish unification.

stories.title: Volkswagen finds defence future for German plant
stories.summary: Volkswagen has struck a preliminary deal that will see one of its German sites switch to defence production under new ownership, a first in the automaker's efforts to restructure plants struggling to compete with lower-cost Chinese rivals. The deal offers a potential blueprint for other Volkswagen sites facing an uncertain future as Europe's largest carmaker embarks on its biggest ever restructuring to revive margins and battle chronic overcapacity in its stagnant European market. Under the initial terms of the deal, Volkswagen will sell its factory in Osnabrueck in its home state of Lower Saxony to Israel's Aurelius Capital, in a move labour officials said could preserve about 1,400 of the site's 1,800 jobs. The agreement comes days after Volkswagen unveiled a major revamp to cut jobs and simplify its structure, highlighting how rising defence spending in Europe could help absorb excess manufacturing capacity in the automotive sector. Volkswagen has warned that up to four German plants could face closure or repurposing unless alternative uses can be found amid weak demand, high costs and growing competition from China. Aurelius Capital and Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, signed a statement of intent yesterday to take over the factory, where vehicle production is due to end in 2027.

stories.title: Russia 'does not rule out' fresh peace talks on Ukraine
stories.summary: Russia does not rule out fresh, three-way talks with Washington and Kyiv on the Ukraine war, the Kremlin has said, after a visit to Moscow and Kyiv by US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. US-led diplomatic efforts to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II have stalled in recent months, as Washington has shifted focus towards the war with Iran. Russian and Ukrainian negotiators last met for US-mediated talks in February, in Geneva, but failed to reach an agreement on the thorny issue of territory. Russia "does not rule out the resumption of the trilateral format, but it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. Mr Witkoff, who is US President Donald Trump's business ally, and Mr Kushner, Mr Trump's son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow - the latest of several visits to the city. A senior Ukrainian presidential source told AFP that the pair had brought "more effective" proposals on ending the war, although neither Moscow and Kyiv announced a breakthrough.

stories.title: Ballydoyle eyeing Group 1 haul across key weekend
stories.summary: Aidan O'Brien is taking nothing for granted as he prepares his galaxy of stars for big-race action on both sides of the Irish Sea this weekend. The Ballydoyle handler has enjoyed another fantastic campaign so far, with his tally of 15 Group 1 winners putting him one ahead of where he was at the same stage nine years ago, when he went on to set a remarkable record of 28 top-level victories in a calendar year. By his own staggering standards, O’Brien has found Group 1 success a little harder to come by in recent weeks, leaving York’s Ebor Festival and the high-profile summer meetings at Deauville without managing to find the bullseye at the highest level. The Phoenix Stakes triumph of Sun Goddess (above) on 9 August was in fact his only Group One win over the course of last month – but with some of his biggest guns set for action over the two-day Irish Champions Festival at Leopardstown and the Curragh, and others heading to Doncaster for the St Leger meeting, it will be a major surprise if he does not increase that tally over the coming days. "Everything leads to this weekend," O’Brien said of two of the biggest days of the season on home soil. "We train the horses hard for the Classics early, then we’ve Royal Ascot and the races in between, where they have to compete because we need the racing miles, but we’re not hard on them and that’s maybe why some were running well without winning – we were leaving a little bit for this weekend.

stories.summary: In the end, it was a very simple equation. Oisín McConville wanted to know that Wicklow still wanted him, Wicklow wanted to know if McConville still wanted them. The first part was an easy yes, but the second was potentially trickier. After Wicklow's brilliant Tailteann Cup triumph, the Armagh man’s stock was never higher. A cluster of county and high-profile club positions awaited him, if he so wished. Wicklow chairman Damien Byrne was also conscious to give his manager as much space as he wanted. McConville's mother Margaret – herself so revered in the Orchard County – died just over a month ago. In the end when the time was right to chat, it was an easy yes for McConville too. Earlier this week it was confirmed that the 2002 All-Ireland winner would take charge of the Garden County for a fifth season. Rarely will Wicklow football look forward to a new season with such enthusiasm. There was the All-Ireland B title in 1992 on the mouth of Christmas under a still-in-his-20s Niall Rennick, the side getting the better of Antrim in Navan.

stories.title: Refreshed Van der Flier ready for World Cup year
stories.summary: Leinster and Ireland flanker Josh van der Flier knows that nothing is won in early September, but that doesn't mean that the 2027 Rugby World Cup escapes the imagination ahead of the start of the 2026/27 season. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU’s new men’s and women’s national team jerseys at the Guinness Open Gate Brewery this week, the 33-year-old was in fine form, which could be attributed to a healthy body and mind. "(I’m) feeling fit as well and getting back into a bit of pre-season stuff and ready for a big few months." This optimistic outlook will come as soothing words to head coach Andy Farrell, who prepares his 12-month plan where all roads hopefully lead to a World Cup final in Sydney on Saturday, 13 November. Van der Flier was part of the two most recent touring squads to Japan in 2019 and France in 2023, where both Irish efforts were ended by the All Blacks. There is a feeling of now or never ahead of the next edition however, but van der Flier insists that he is taking the coming months one at a time. "It's always tempting to start thinking of those (major tournaments), but it's obviously like how rugby goes, it tends to be week-to-week and you've got to look after your pre-season first," he said.

stories.title: 100 Buildings: Machine House - Ardnacrusha's iconic Power Station
stories.summary: One of the first major infrastructure projects for the Free State was the Shannon hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, Co. Clare. It involved the construction of a huge dam and a power station, the scale of which had never been seen before, to harness the waters of the River Shannon to power a national electric grid. This far-seeing civil engineering project would eventually enable the rural electrification of Ireland. The idea of the Shannon Scheme was the brainchild of a young Irish engineer, Dr Thomas A. McLaughlin (1896-1971), who had worked as a graduate for Siemens-Schucker in Berlin in 1922 (1). He returned to Ireland the following year with a proposal for Siemens to implement this electricity expansion to the Irish government. His Shannon Scheme was more productive and cost-effective than the Dublin-centred plan, based on the River Liffey, which was then being considered (2). The contract for the construction work was awarded to Siemens in 1925. The power station had, as Seán Rotherty writes, a 'truly Germanic look' in its utility with its high-pitched roof with tiny dormer windows in its double attic. The large steel-framed and concrete-walled power station has an impressive industrial look devoid of ornamentation. It is a monumental complex of transformer rooms, control rooms, switch houses and cooling houses but they are interconnected to give the streamlined appearance of a single building. The dam/sluice house to the rear of the power station has a flat roof with a T-shaped plan. The power station is a protected structure on the Clare County Council Development Plan (RPS No. 311). The Electricity Supply Board (ESB) was created to manage the new station in 1927 with Dr Thomas A. McLaughlin appointed as its first managing director. The Shannon Scheme was operational in 19293, producing almost all of Ireland’s electricity needs. It was one of the largest hydroelectric stations in the world, creating 3,000 jobs and costing about 20 per cent of the government expenditure. The Shannon Scheme formally opened on 22 July 1929. The legacy of the German engineering at Ardnacrusha is present today with the standard electric voltage in Ireland at 220 volts following the German system, as opposed to 240 volts in the UK (4). The Shannon power station continues to produce electricity but its output is today only a tiny percentage of the national electricity production. It changed the Irish landscape physically with substations and generators as well as poles, pylons and wires, metaphorically bringing modernity and ambition to the fledging Free State. Thank you to photographer John Glynn for his generous use of his photographs and to Dermot Finnan of ESB. Read more entries from the 100 Buildings series here.

stories.title: Trailer for The Lost Children of Tuam released
stories.summary: The trailer for The Lost Children of Tuam, the new drama about local historian Catherine Corless and her research into the former mother-and-baby home in Tuam, Co Galway, has been released ahead of the film's arrival in cinemas later this month. Research by Catherine Corless found that there were no burial records for almost 800 babies and infants who died at the home over a 36-year period. stories.title: Conor Pope's tips for saving money at home this winter
stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. Additionally, the need to tumble dry clothes can be a big expense, alongside buying warmer clothing, extra food, and saving up for Christmas presents. "I've done the maths, and I reckon that winter time costs about €10,000 more for the average household than summer time," he states. "That's not even being wildly extravagant." The first step in bringing those costs down? Shopping around for an electricity provider. "The reality is that more than 70% of Irish consumers don't switch their energy provider," the savvy saver explains, "despite the fact that, even in a climate of rising prices, you can still knock about €500 off your annual bill - just by moving from company A to company B." Many people will avoid switching because it feels like too much hassle, but Pope insists that sites like Bonkers.ie and Switcher.ie make it incredibly straightforward.

stories.title: Rise in child poverty despite growth in average incomes
stories.summary: One in 10 children are deprived of basic necessities as Ireland sees a sharp rise in child poverty despite a strong growth in average incomes, research suggests. New ESRI research published today shows that child poverty is on the rise despite strong growth in average household incomes, with 200,000 children living in households below the poverty line. It also shows that the benefits of rising incomes are not being shared evenly. The number of children in households below the poverty line, which is defined as having less than 60% of median household income, increased by almost 30,000 children in 2024. This increase is despite strong growth in average household income, which when adjusted for inflation, household size and composition, rose by 4% between 2023 and 2024. The rise in child poverty was larger after housing costs were accounted for, rising by 40,000 to 260,000 children (22.7%). The increase was particularly pronounced for families with young children, rising from 20.8% to 26.6% for families whose youngest child was five years old and younger when housing costs were accounted for.

stories.title: Public sector craft workers to take industrial action
stories.summary: Craft workers in the public sector, who provide services in areas such as electrical and plumbing, are to take industrial action later this month in a dispute over pay. The workers are represented by the Public Sector Craft Group of Unions (PSCGOU), which is made up of Connect, Unite, SIPTU, BATU and OPTASI. According to the unions, craft worker in the public sector have significantly lower earnings compared with their private sector colleagues. "A recent independent review of craft pay found that workers in the public sector were paid, on average, €4.40 less per hour than their colleagues in the private sector," said Connect Public Service Official, Brian McAvinue. "In recent weeks we have balloted our members throughout the public service, with a resounding vote in favour of industrial action, up to and including strike action." "These workers provide vital electrical, plumbing and other essential craft skills throughout our health, local authority and governmental services," Mr McAvinue said.

stories.title: Presidential talks wedged within Trump's golf appearance
stories.summary: Unlike US presidents who came before him, Donald Trump's visit to Ireland this week is about the fairways, rather than searching for roots. While it is unlikely he'll pose with a pint of the black stuff in an ancestral home like Barack Obama or Ronald Reagan, or name a family pet after a village in Ireland (Richard Nixon had an Irish setter called King Timahoe), Mr Trump will be welcomed by hundreds of locals and tens of thousands of golf fans at the Amgen Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg. Much of his weekend will be spent at the event in west Clare, where it is expected he will present the trophy to the Irish Open winner on Sunday. But just because the avid golfer has limited political engagements - with the trip being personal rather than an official state visit - doesn't mean it will be a quiet or unassuming affair. After teasing the visit for months, President Trump is expected to land in Dublin on Saturday morning aboard his new Air Force One, the aircraft given to him by Qatar, and he will be greeted by Tánaiste Simon Harris. The Phoenix Park is set to become something of a political fortress, with a high-security operation in place by the end of the week, as Mr Trump starts his weekend with a visit to Deerfield Residence, the official residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland.

stories.title: Uniphar on track to meet full year growth objectives
stories.summary: Healthcare services provider Uniphar has reported higher revenues and profits for the six months to the end of June and said it remains on track to meet its growth objectives for the rest of the year. Uniphar owns Allcare Pharmacy, Hickey's Pharmacy and McCauley Health and Beauty here. Its half year revenues rose by 7.2% to €1.592 billion from €1.485 billion the same time last year, while its profit before tax grew by 8.5% to €31.14m from €28.7m. The Uniphar board has declared an interim dividend of €0.0074 per ordinary share for the six months to June 30, an increase of 4.2% on the same time last year. Breaking down its divisions, its Uniphar Pharma unit reported 7% organic gross profit growth against a strong previous year comparator, supported by continued progress across Global Sourcing and Pharma Services. Its Uniphar Medtech division posted 9% organic gross profit growth supported by broad-based demand across core specialisms, portfolio expansion into new markets and continued enhancement of the product offering.

stories.title: Panama Canal may further reduce crossings due to El Niño
stories.summary: The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Niño weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway has said. Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Niño, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures. This year's El Niño is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago. Panama's restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel. The interoceanic Panama Canal - which handles five percent of global maritime trade - has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September. It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino.

stories.title: Gauff overcomes jittery start to progress, Osaka bows out
stories.summary: Coco Gauff won the all-American Labour Day showdown against teenager Iva Jovic to reach the US Open quarter-finals. The 22-year-old, bidding for a second Flushing Meadows title, overpowered Jovic 6-1 6-4 on a balmy bank holiday night in New York. An impressive victory set up a last-eight meeting with French Open champion Mirra Andreeva, whom Gauff has beaten in all five of their career meetings. A jittery start from the 2023 winner gifted 18-year-old Jovic a break in the first game with a double fault. But Jovic's nerves were also on show as Gauff raced away with the next six games to take the first set. Jovic finally held serve at the start of the second but three spectacular Gauff hustles, turning desperate defence into all-out attack, secured a break for 3-2.
